Perhaps it’s time to ask whether the concept of Capital has ended up being rather more of a theological production than Marx would have intended. Hence Capital is Dead proceeds along two lines at once. It makes a minimally plausible case that the thesis of a new mode of production is worth investigating, and at the same time it is a critical account of how we got stuck trying to explain all emerging phenomena as if they were always expressions of the same eternal essence of Capital.

Capital is Dead. Long Live Capital! A Political Marxist Analysis of Digital Capitalism and Infrastructure

Authors

* Maïa Pal Oxford Brookes University 
* Neal Harris Oxford Brookes University 

DOI:

Keywords:

digital capitalism, infrastructure, mode of production, vectoralism, McKenzie Wark, imperialism, political Marxism

Abstract

There is a growing literature suggesting that the digital economy is taking us out of capitalism. While this manifests most notably as a diagnosis of ‘digital feudalism’ or ‘techno-feudalism’, a differing voice is McKenzie Wark, who suggests we have entered an entirely new mode of production altogether: ‘vectoralism’. This paper historicises and theorises our current conjuncture in relation to the potential multiplicity of modes of production, and the materiality and imperialism of telecommunication infrastructures. We approve of Wark's development of new concepts, rather than turning to ahistorical regurgitations like ‘neo-feudalism’. However, we argue that the mode of production lens is not adequate to trace what we consider as more granular changes and that it risks packaging old wine in new bottles.
